title: The Closest Thing We Have to Alien Technology
beats: Zoom into a chip: a city of skyscraper layers over billions of transistors; Moore's Law stalled around 2015, one company saved it
Thought experiment: shrunk to ant size with a laser, hit a tin droplet three times in 20 microseconds, 50,000 droplets a second
Mirrors smooth to a playing-card bump on an Earth-size surface; overlay within five atoms; 30 years called impossible
Quick aside: ASML did not sponsor this video
Chip fabrication in four steps: coat, expose, etch, deposit; repeat 10-100 layers
Photolithography flagged as hardest step because it sets feature size
Real reticle plus red laser pointer shows diffraction; two-gap picture for in-phase and out-of-phase
Designers use diffraction rather than fight it; need zero and first orders captured
Numerical aperture as sin of angle, limit of one; green laser dots sit closer than red, so shorter wavelength wins; Rayleigh equation named
Industry settles at 193 nm deep UV; Moore's Law about to hit a wall
Kinoshita 1980s: use 10 nm x-rays, but air and lenses absorb them; vacuum and mirrors needed
Multilayer mirror: quarter-wavelength layers, phase flip, 76 alternating layers add constructively; only 6% reflected but proof of principle
Kinoshita prints 4-micron lines, audience calls it a fish story
Two obstacles: no natural light source (synchrotron the size of a soccer field) and mirrors must be atomically smooth
Football vs bouncy ball on cobblestones: roughness compared to scale; household mirror bumps 4000 atoms, needed 2.3; Germany-size mirror with 1 mm bump
Livermore and Andy Hawryluk: laughed off stage in 1988, then Bell Labs call; labs pivot to commercial partners; 1996 funding cut; Intel and others pay $250M
Engineering Test Stand 2000: 9.8 W, eight mirrors, prints 70 nm but only about 10 wafers an hour
Light budget: 70% per mirror, nine bounces leaves 4%; six mirrors plus reticle leaves 8%; need 100 W source
American firms leave; ASML (Philips spin-off, Zeiss partner) takes it on
Choosing wavelength: 4 nm leaves 0.00128% after bounces, Mo/Be best but toxic, so Si/Mo at 13.5 nm
Sputtered mirror layers are bumpy; ion beam shakes atoms into holes
Three ways to make EUV: synchrotron, discharge plasma (could not scale), laser plasma
Xenon fails (0.5% efficiency); tin is 5-10x better but neutral tin absorbs, so one droplet at a time, 50,000 a second
Tin jet: vibrating nozzle, irregular droplets merge into regular ones, 'magic sauce' of modulation
Tin debris coats a mirror; hydrogen flow forms stannane to clean it, but too much hydrogen absorbs light and overheats
Ultra-fast camera shows shockwave; Taylor-von Neumann-Sedov formula for nuclear blasts and supernovae fits exactly; mini supernovae 50,000 times a second
Heat shifts mirrors; Zeiss sensors hold pico-radian accuracy: laser pointer aimed at a dime on the Moon
Tin too dense; ASML starts next-gen high NA in 2012 and gets customers to invest billions; humor: candles lit in a chapel correlate with power
Pre-pulse flattens droplet into pancake, main pulse vaporizes it; 100 W in 2014; moving goalposts; 200 W demonstrated as board lands in Korea
Golf ball must land in the hole every time; laser curtains time the shot
Collector mirrors needed cleaning every 10 hours; an engineer notices opening the machine cleans mirrors; add a little oxygen; commercially viable by 2016
Low NA vs high NA (0.33 vs 0.55); clean room tour; light source module; pulses per droplet; 20 G reticle; 1 nm overlay budget shared across teams
5,000 suppliers, 100,000 parts, 250 containers, 7 Boeing 747s to ship
Bet made in 2001, first customer system 2010, first phone 2019
Closing essay: the reasonable people were right on facts, progress depends on the unreasonable man
Brilliant sponsor read tied to learning by doing

new_moves.name: scale-ladder-analogies
new_moves.what: Express precision with a scaled-up familiar object (smoothness as Earth or Germany with card or millimeter bump; laser to dime on Moon) and reuse the same device for the high NA upgrade

new_moves.name: human-stake-story-as-spine
new_moves.what: Tell dissent and repeated rejection of named people as the narrative spine that holds the technical sections together

new_moves.name: physics-reuse-surprise
new_moves.what: Show a formula from another field (nuclear blast, supernova) fitting this system to get the viewer to feel the physics is universal

new_moves.name: debug-by-accident
new_moves.what: Fix arrives from someone noticing something odd while the system was opened (oxygen cleaning)

theory: The video wraps a dense optics lecture inside a thirty-year underdog story and uses a repeating loop of 'need, attempt, failure, fix' so each technical idea is earned as the solution to a visible obstacle. Concepts that need math (diffraction, NA, multilayer reflection) are anchored on a physical demo or analogy first and named late. Scale comparisons make precision feel graspable.
velocity: Scene builder: reusable 'obstacle then fix' template with a running constraint counter (watts, wafers per hour) that updates visibly.
Orchestrator: introduce notation only after a demo (laser pointer, then NA at 7:17); gate formula scenes on a demonstrated need.
Voice: story beats should carry naming of people as characters; the learner-model can pick story-heavy versions for engaged learners.
Evals: check scale analogies that reuse one device (Earth, Germany) across the lesson.
Ghost hands: highlight the two-slit pattern while narrating in-phase/out-of-phase.
quote: The reasonable thing is to think that none of that is possible
